title: Tree canopy and neighborhood cooling in urban heat islands
abstract: Neighborhoods with higher tree canopy often show lower daytime surface temperature, but effects depend on water availability, canopy continuity, and street geometry.

fixture_excerpts: Tree canopy is associated with lower daytime surface temperature through shade and evapotranspiration, but cooling varies with canopy continuity and water availability.

title: Context-dependent cooling from reflective roofs
abstract: Reflective roofs reduce roof surface temperature and building heat gain. The pedestrian-level cooling benefit can be smaller or mixed when reflected radiation and urban geometry are unfavorable.

fixture_excerpts: Reflective roofs reduce roof surface temperature, although pedestrian-level benefits can be mixed when reflected radiation is trapped by street geometry.

title: Impervious cover and nighttime heat retention
abstract: High impervious cover and low vegetation are associated with higher nighttime air temperature because stored heat is released slowly after sunset.

fixture_excerpts: Impervious surfaces store heat during the day and release it at night, contributing to persistent nighttime heat exposure.

title: Sensor placement bias in neighborhood heat measurements
abstract: Sparse or poorly placed sensors can exaggerate apparent intervention effects if shaded, ventilated, or atypical locations are oversampled.

fixture_excerpts: Measurement design can create apparent cooling differences when sensors are unevenly placed in shaded, ventilated, or otherwise atypical micro-sites.
